docs.title: python-repo-template
docs.text:
A baseline for new Python projects, with the most commonly used tools and community best practices set up and wired together. Projects made from it stay in sync with it: the template's later changes reach them through template_sync.py update.

  • Getting started: create a project from the template.
  • Staying in sync: bring the template's later changes into a project.
  • Config system: how a project's settings and secrets work.
  • Private dependencies: let CI and Dependabot read private git dependencies.
  • Container job: run the package as a scheduled Azure Container Apps job.
  • Changing the template: for the template's maintainers.

The source is at github.com/DrollRobot/python_repo_template.

docs.title: Changing the template
docs.text: For the template's maintainers.

docs.title: Classifying files
docs.text:
• Classify every new tracked file in template.toml, under [base] or the feature it belongs to.
  • Files only projects get live under child/, which [paths] maps to the project's root: child/README.md becomes the project's README.md.
  • Moving a file in the template is safe as long as it still lands on the same project path: update treats the new path as the old file, and merges against the old path's content.
  • The template's own README, mkdocs.yml and docs/ (this site) are excluded: projects get child/mkdocs.yml and child/docs/ instead. Files a project ships can't link to this site, because token substitution would rewrite the URL; they name the page instead, as docs/<page>.md in the template.

docs.title: Keeping parts of a file out of child projects
docs.text: Wrap anything that must not reach projects in a <template-only> block: a line holding only the tag in the file's comment syntax (# <template-only> ... # </template-only>). Tagged blocks (feature="mkdocs", feature="!mkdocs", feature="a|b") reach only the projects whose features match.

docs.title: Moving to a new Python release
docs.text: When Python ships a release (in October, when the oldest version also reaches end of life), move the version tokens in template.toml and their literals in the files together: .python-version, pyproject.toml, the CI matrix, the badges and CONTRIBUTING.md. The all-supported aliases list the maintained versions. tests/test_template_manifest.py fails on any literal left behind.

docs.title: Checking your changes
docs.text:
• uv run scripts/template_sync.py validate checks all of the above; the pre-commit hook and CI run it too.
  • CI also makes four projects from the template (defaults, every feature off, every feature on, a library) and runs each one's gates. Run the same check locally with uv run pytest tests/test_template_manifest.py -m live.
  • uv run mkdocs build --strict builds this site.

docs.title: Config system
docs.text:
With the config_system feature on, a project's package gets a config package (src/<package>/config/): per-user settings that live outside the repo, a command to manage them, and, with secret_storage on, secrets kept in a credential store instead of a file.

The examples below are for a project named my-widget: package my_widget, config command my-widget-config, environment variable prefix MY_WIDGET_.

docs.title: Where settings live
docs.text:
Each user's settings live in a config.toml in the operating system's standard per-user config folder, never in the repo:

OS Location Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\my_widget\config.toml Linux ~/.config/my_widget/config.toml (respects XDG_CONFIG_HOME) macOS ~/Library/Application Support/my_widget/config.toml

MY_WIDGET_CONFIG_DIR moves the folder elsewhere, for tests and portable installs. my-widget-config path prints where the file is.

docs.title: Defining settings
docs.text:
src/my_widget/config/schema.py defines every setting, in one dataclass, Settings. Each field is declared with option() or secret():

  • option(help=..., default_value=...) is a plain setting. Without a default_value, it is required.
  • secret(help=...) is a secret. It has no default, since secret values never appear in source, so it is always required.

Everything else follows from the fields: the config command's prompts, the file's validation, the environment variable names, and the tests' fake configurations. To add, rename or remove a setting, edit Settings and nothing else. The template's example fields (tenant_id, client_id, api_url, ...) are placeholders to replace.

docs.title: Reading settings in code
docs.text:
from my_widget.config import load_settings

settings = load_settings()  # or load_settings(profile="contoso")
settings.api_url

docs.title: Where each value comes from
docs.text:
load_settings takes each field from the first of these that has it:

  1. Explicit overrides passed by the calling code, for example from command-line flags.
  2. An environment variable: MY_WIDGET_ plus the field's name in capitals, such as MY_WIDGET_API_URL. This is the path for CI and other headless runs: it needs no file and no credential store.
  3. The credential store, for secret fields only (see Secrets).
  4. config.toml: the selected profile's table, then the file's top-level keys.
  5. The field's default, for plain settings only.

A required value missing from every layer raises an error that names the fix. load_settings never creates the file and never falls back silently.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
One file can hold settings for several tenants or environments. Top-level keys act as shared fallbacks:

# Single profile: bare top-level keys.
tenant_id = "..."

# Several profiles. Top-level keys are shared fallbacks.
default_profile = "contoso"

[profiles.contoso]
tenant_id = "..."

The profile in use is the first of: the profile argument to load_settings, the MY_WIDGET_PROFILE environment variable, the file's default_profile, else the top-level keys as one unnamed profile.

The file is validated strictly: an unknown key, a secret value written into the file, or a malformed table stops the program with an error naming the problem.

docs.title: The config command
docs.text:
my-widget-config (also python -m my_widget.config) creates and edits the file, so it never needs editing by hand. It keeps the comments in the file.

Command What it does init Interactive first-time setup: prompts for each setting from the schema. --force starts the file over. path Print the file's location. open Open the file in the program the OS associates with it. show The effective settings, with secrets masked and where each value came from. set KEY VALUE Write a plain setting. unset KEY Remove a setting, so its default applies again. list-profiles List the profiles, marking the default. use PROFILE Set default_profile. set-secret KEY Store a secret (see below). delete-secret KEY Remove a secret from the credential store.

The two secret commands exist only when the schema has secret fields and its CREDENTIAL_BACKEND isn't "none".

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
With secret_storage on, secret values live in a credential store, never in config.toml or on the command line, where shell history would keep them. The file holds only each secret's storage name (<field>_secret_name), which is not itself secret. init and set-secret ask for the name in plain view and for the value hidden.

CREDENTIAL_BACKEND in schema.py sets the policy:

  • "prompt" (the template's default): no default store; the user picks one with credential_backend in config.toml, through init or set.
  • a store's name, such as "keyring": that store, unless a profile picks another with credential_backend.
  • "none": the package stores no secrets. Environment variables still work.

Two stores ship, each its own feature:

  • keyring (the keyring feature): the OS credential store, which is Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain, or the Linux Secret Service. Secrets are filed per profile, under the service my_widget:<profile> (or my_widget for the unnamed profile). On a machine with no usable store (a container, CI, Linux without a Secret Service) it stops with an error; it never falls back to writing secrets to a file.
  • keyvault (the keyvault feature): Azure Key Vault, read-only. A profile sets credential_backend = "keyvault" and keyvault_url. It signs in with DefaultAzureCredential (az login, a managed identity, or service principal variables) and keeps values in memory only. Change secrets in the Azure portal or with az keyvault secret set. Key Vault names can't hold underscores, so client_secret is looked up as client-secret.

Each store's packages are an optional extra, so users install only the one they use: pip install my-widget[keyring], or uv sync --extra keyring.

docs.title: Leaving parts out
docs.text:
Each part is a feature you can decline at new:

  • config_system off: no config package at all.
  • secret_storage off: settings without secrets. The secret machinery is left out, and secret-related keys are illegal in config.toml.
  • keyring or keyvault off: that store is left out, with its optional dependencies.

docs.title: Container job
docs.text: With the container_job feature on, a project can run its package as a scheduled Azure Container Apps job. The feature ships the image build (Dockerfile), its workflow (.github/workflows/image.yml), and scripts/container_job.py, which creates the job and everything it needs.

docs.title: 1. Check the package can run unattended
docs.text:
In a container, nobody answers prompts. Check that the package:

  • Resolves its settings with no config.toml: from defaults, or from environment variables set on the job ([job.env] in the job's config file). See Config system.
  • Reads secrets through the job's managed identity: the Key Vault backend's DefaultAzureCredential picks the identity from an AZURE_CLIENT_ID variable on the job.
  • Logs to the console. Log Analytics keeps the output; the package needs no log file.
  • Never prompts or opens a browser.
  • Imports every module on <entrypoint> --help: that is the image's smoke test.

docs.title: 2. Create the job
docs.text:
Copy scripts/container_job.example.toml somewhere outside the repo's tracked files, fill it in, and run the setup with an account that can grant roles:

uv run scripts/container_job.py path/to/your.toml --dry-run
uv run scripts/container_job.py path/to/your.toml

It creates whatever is missing (the shared resources, the job's identities and roles, the job, the repo variables, the failed-run alert) and updates whatever differs from the file. To change a setting later, edit the file and run it again.

docs.title: 3. How the image gets there
docs.text: The job starts on Microsoft's quickstart image. Each push to main then builds the package's image, publishes it, and points the job at it. A scheduled run also rebuilds main weekly on a freshly pulled base image; the cron in image.yml sets how often.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Making a project from the template takes three steps; the last sections cover what depends on the features you keep.

docs.title: 1. Clone the template
docs.text: git clone https://github.com/DrollRobot/python_repo_template.git

docs.title: 2. Create the project
docs.text:
From the template folder:

uv run scripts/template_sync.py new ../<new repo name>

It asks which optional features to keep, and which license to use: MIT (the default), Apache 2.0, GPL 3.0, proprietary, or none, which leaves out the LICENSE file. Then it asks for each value that --set didn't give and the project's files use:

  • the project name (default: the directory's name). Any of My Widget, my-widget or my_widget gives both the my_widget package and the my-widget distribution.
  • your GitHub user (no default).
  • the Python version.
  • whatever the chosen license names: the copyright holder and year, and for the proprietary license, also the company.

The Python version defaults to the newest, 3.15, which the template always targets. A version such as 3.13 pins the project to exactly that Python (requires-python = "==3.13.*", CI on 3.13 alone). all-supported makes a library: it supports every Python version still maintained (3.11 to 3.15 today), develops and type-checks on the oldest, and CI tests all of them.

-y takes every default without asking; --feature NAME=false turns a feature off. The target must not exist, or be empty, or be an empty git repository (as cloning a newly created GitHub repo leaves). It writes the project, runs git init on main, and stages everything.

Then it bootstraps the project, running the commands under [new] in template.toml: it sets the version to 0.1.0, runs uv sync (writing uv.lock), scans for secrets into .secrets.baseline, installs the pre-commit and pre-push hooks, and stages the result. It commits nothing. --no-bootstrap skips this and prints the commands instead; if a command fails, new stops there and prints the ones left.

docs.title: 3. Finish the setup
docs.text:
In the new project:

cd ../my-widget
uv run detect-secrets audit .secrets.baseline    # mark each finding real or false
git grep -n FIXME                                # placeholders left for you to fill in
git commit

The pre-commit hooks refuse the commit until every baseline entry is audited.

Then write some code. To bring in the template's later changes, see Staying in sync.

docs.title: If you kept mkdocs
docs.text:
Enable GitHub Pages for the project's docs: in the GitHub repo's settings, set the Pages source to the gh-pages branch. Then deploy:

uv run mkdocs gh-deploy --force

The workflow in .github/workflows/docs.yml keeps the site updated on later pushes to main.

docs.title: If the project has private git dependencies
docs.text: CI and Dependabot need credentials to read them: see Private dependencies.

docs.title: If you want to run the project as an Azure Container Job
docs.text: With container_job on, the package runs as a scheduled Azure Container Apps job: see Container job.

docs.title: If the project has settings
docs.text: With config_system on, the package reads its settings from a per-user config.toml: see Config system.

docs.title: Private dependencies
docs.text:
A project whose dependencies include private git repos needs credentials for CI and Dependabot to read them. With the private_repo_deps feature on, the project's workflows carry the steps that use them. Those steps skip until the repo has the GH_APP_CLIENT_ID variable, so CI works before the setup and picks the credentials up after it. .github/dependabot.yml can't skip a step, so its registry ships commented out. The steps below create the credentials and turn Dependabot's registry on.

CI reads the private repos with a GitHub App's token. Dependabot can't use the App when it updates uv.lock, so it gets its own fine-grained personal access token.

docs.title: 1. Create the GitHub App
docs.text:
In the GitHub account: Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New.

  • Permissions → Repository permissions → Contents: Read-only (Metadata: Read is added automatically). Nothing else.
  • Webhook → uncheck Active (the App needs no events).
  • Where can this be installed → Only on this account.

docs.title: 2. Make a private key
docs.text: On the App's page, choose "Generate a private key" and download the .pem file. Note the Client ID shown at the top of the page.

docs.title: 3. Install the App
docs.text: Install it onto the private repos it reads: Org Settings → the App → Install → select repositories.

docs.title: 4. List the private repos in the workflows
docs.text:
Each token step in .github/workflows/ ends with a placeholder list (git grep -n "FIXME list the private repos" finds them):

owner: ""
repositories: private-repo-1, private-repo-2

Replace the placeholder with the private repos' names, comma-separated. The token CI mints reads only those repos.

owner: "" means the project repo's owner. For repos under another owner, set owner: to it, and keep the list non-empty: an owner with an empty list gives the token every repo the App is installed on.

docs.title: 5. Save the App's credentials in the project
docs.text:
In the project's repo. The key is saved twice because Dependabot's CI runs can't read the repo's other secrets.

gh secret set GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY < path/to/app.private-key.pem
gh secret set GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY --app dependabot < path/to/app.private-key.pem
gh variable set GH_APP_CLIENT_ID --body "<app client id>"

Get-Content -Raw path\to\app.private-key.pem | gh secret set GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY
Get-Content -Raw path\to\app.private-key.pem | gh secret set GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY --app dependabot
gh variable set GH_APP_CLIENT_ID --body "<app client id>"

From the next run on, CI mints a token and reads the private repos.

docs.title: 6. Give Dependabot its own token
docs.text:
Create a fine-grained personal access token: Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens.

  • Resource owner → the account that owns the private repos.
  • Repository access → Only select repositories → the private repos the project depends on.
  • Permissions → Repository permissions → Contents: Read-only. Nothing else.
  • Expiration → set one, and note when to rotate it.

Save it in the project's repo (gh prompts for the value):

gh secret set DEPENDABOT_GIT_TOKEN --app dependabot

docs.title: 7. Turn on Dependabot's registry
docs.text: Uncomment both blocks that start with # FIXME uncomment in .github/dependabot.yml.

docs.title: 8. Update the token action
docs.text: Pin actions/create-github-app-token to its latest trusted commit.

docs.title: Staying in sync
docs.text: A child project carries one file from the template: .template.toml. It records the template commit it was last synced to, its values, its feature choices and any per-file overrides. If you prefer not to have the .template.toml in git history, the sync script will also find it at .local/.template.toml.

docs.title: Bringing in the template's changes
docs.text:
git pull
uv run scripts/template_sync.py check ../my-widget    # shows what would change
uv run scripts/template_sync.py update ../my-widget   # apply changes

docs.title: What each file gets
docs.text:
template.toml decides:

  • managed files belong to the template: update brings them to the template's version, and check reports local edits as drift.
  • merge files are edited on both sides (pyproject.toml, AGENTS.md, .gitignore, ...): update 3-way merges the template's changes into the project's copy, and leaves conflict markers, like git, when both sides changed the same lines.
  • seed files (README.md, src/<package>/main.py, ...) are written once, by new. update --seed installs seed files the template has added since.

docs.title: Forking a managed file
docs.text: A project that forks a managed file for good sets, for example, "src/my_widget/config/cli.py" = "merge" (or "ignore") under [overrides] in .template.toml.

docs.title: Moving to another Python version
docs.text: A project keeps the Python version it was created with when the template moves on. To move it, change python in .template.toml and run update, which rewrites the managed files. Then make the same change by hand in the merge files that name the version (pyproject.toml, .python-version, and CONTRIBUTING.md if you have it), since update keeps your copies of those.
